title: Private Equity-Owned Psychiatric Hospitals Might Be Safer?!?
subtitle: A lesson in how not to write an academic paper
body_html:
Oh my gosh, this newsletter has been investigating private equity and its role in healthcare for some time. Just yesterday, we read a paper in JAMA Psychiatry about the role of private equity in freestanding psychiatric hospitals. Oh my gosh, was it surprising? It was! However, unless you read it closely, it's less conclusive.

It has a catchy title:

Private Equity Among US Psychiatric Hospitals

The paper reviewed the data on every freestanding psychiatric hospital in the country. Every single one of them. There are 617, for those keeping track. Of those, 87 are owned by private equity. That's 14.10%. Shields and colleagues have the information available, publicly, on those hospitals.1 They found that the staffing ratios were lower in private equity hospitals, which probably doesn't surprise anybody.

Here were their outcomes, as enumerated in the paper:

Main outcomes were staffing ratios, national quality measures (restraint and seclusion rates, 7- and 30-day follow-up rates, postdischarge medication continuation, and 30-day all-cause readmission rates). Other studied characteristics included institutional characteristics (region, number of beds), services provided, measures of case mix (populations served, hospital average Diagnosis Related Group score among Medicare beneficiaries), occupancy rates, and average length of stay.

And it was a little shocking to see that the private equity-owned hospitals did better on the outcome metrics they looked at:

Yet, PE-owned facilities performed better on quality measures, including lower reported hours of restraint use (0.03 vs 0.24 hours per 1000 patient hours; P < .001), 30-day readmissions (19.40% vs 20.16%; P = .047), and higher 7-day (29.34% vs 26.28%; P = .03) and 30-day (52.92% vs 49.08%; P = .01) follow-up visits.

How could this be? Was private equity really doing a great job of running private psychiatric hospitals?

Spoiler alert, I don't think that's the case. And I will explain why I don't think that's the case, in a causal direction. The last quality metric, the follow-up visit number, is the easiest to address. I firmly believe that Private psychiatric hospitals owned by Private equity are highly incentivized to have higher follow-up visit rates because they want to make money from those follow-up visits. That's easy to believe. Credit where it’s due—good job, free-standing psychiatric hospitals owned by PE, on all of this.

However, lower use of restraint and lower 30-day readmissions? What could be causing these better outcomes, especially after those bad guys in suits get involved?

One possibility is that the bad guys and suits aren't so bad. Maybe bringing a little bit of rigor and structure, from the guys in the business suits, is helpful to driving psychiatric care in the right direction. This is one possible reading of the study. And the opposite, that private equity made these hospitals worse, that's not a conclusion we can draw.

But the details matter here. Let me walk you through my thinking. I am very suspicious of private equity. Some of you may think, Owen, you're actively involved in litigation with the people (like Amanda Itzkoff, M.D., and Jack Wolcowitz) who acquired your prior practice. You've got a bone to pick, Muir! Yes, that would be a grievance I am leaving to the courts to settle. Many of my colleagues have had negative experiences with private equity, and the data, as I’ve previously written, is not good.

However, this data is different. Private equity-owned freestanding psychiatric hospitals appear to do better than non-private equity-owned freestanding psychiatric hospitals when it comes to quality measures in this sample…how could that be?

Not all psychiatric units are freestanding hospitals. Most aren't. Most psychiatric units are inside general medical hospitals. Psychiatric hospitals, as I've written previously, have a history of harms that are hard to capture in this sort of data. People end up in a psychiatric hospital because they're a danger to themselves or others, on average. But how dangerous are they? That's a question that matters. How dangerous are they in the psychiatric hospital itself? So out of sorts that they end up needing restraint or seclusion? That's usually not the kind of problem. You're seeing with people who are cripplingly, depressed, or suicidal. That's usually a problem that is secondary to agitation. And agitation is more likely to be due to substance use disorder, psychotic disorder, bipolar disorder, delirium, or any of those kinds of problems. Not depression, and not feeling suicidal. Those individuals are generally pretty low, energy-wise, and not being restrained. The risk is that they will fake it till they make it out of the hospital, and then die by suicide later—an outcome hospitals might make worse, not better.

Now, one would imagine that they would capture what kind of patients are in these hospitals, and you'd be wrong.

An important caveat in this publication is that they don't have the patient-level data—this means they don't have the individual diagnoses on which people were admitted, which could say “major depressive disorder, recurrent, severe, without psychotic features.” Or it could say “schizophrenia.” They had none of that data. They only looked at hospitals that accepted Medicare, and they used Medicare. DRG codes to stratify the patients as to why they came into the hospital.

This Medicare DRG-based data, a problematic system regarding reimbursement2, is woefully insufficient for this use case! Here is the level of detail captured by a diagnostic reference group, or DRG, in a psychiatric hospital admission…

So for example, major depressive disorder that severe, that's an 855. Any psychiatric diagnosis that is less severe? You get it, it's just about medical comorbidity, and a little bit about severity, but no actual granular detail. All which is not enough to tell you if the private freestanding psychiatric hospital is screening in or outpatient that they don't want in their facility. They might be cherry picking. If I were them, I would be cherry picking. I would not let in the difficult patients who are gonna cause a ruckus and lead to restraint, I would want to have a hospital that screens for less psychiatrically, unwell people. Or at least more quietly unwell, psychiatrically ill people.

And there's a reason for this—you can get them out of the hospital after their paid days have expired, and most of these hospitals have a contract that pays per day. The ideal patient for this purpose is one who's not very sick. You can keep them to the very end of their paid days, and then you can kick them out because they're feeling better… or never needed to be there in the first place.

So what I suspect was happening in this dataset is pretty simple: freestanding psychiatric hospitals screen for people that they could hold against their will for as long as it made financial sense, and then when it didn't make financial sense, they could discharge them without worrying. We know from reports on Acadia, the publicly traded company accused of doing this in the media, that they make a lot of money. And they do it by holding people on fake involuntary holds until they can switch them to voluntary discharges.

They don't do it by forcibly, hospitalizing, dangerous, or violent people who are going to need a restraint, because then you need a higher staffing ratio, and you'd have more restraints and seclusions.

Since this paper didn't report on any of the details of the patient level information about what kind of diagnoses these hospitals were treating, and they got by with lower staffing ratios…to remind us:

In adjusted models, PE ownership was associated with significantly lower staff per patient day among registered nurses (0.12 vs 0.15; P = .048 and medical social workers (0.02 vs 0.04; P = .005).

It makes perfect sense that they had lower rates of restraint, readmission, and money-making follow-ups. How do you guarantee lower readmission rates? Hospitalize people who don't need to be there in the first place.

In The New York Times report, Acadia Healthcare is said to have routinely held patients longer than was necessary and often against their will at certain facilities. The report also claims Acadia would trump up patient symptoms in reports to payers to extract more reimbursement.

Those people have a good sense to fake feeling better until you let them out, and then they never want to return. And here's what the data looks like if you use that strategy:

lower reported hours of restraint use (0.03 vs 0.24 hours per 1000 patient hours; P < .001), 30-day readmissions (19.40% vs 20.16%; P = .047), and higher 7-day (29.34% vs 26.28%; P = .03) and 30-day (52.92% vs 49.08%; P = .01) follow-up visits.

Inpatient psychiatry is all about the patients you admit. And if you choose who you admit, you can cherry-pick patients who meet your resources, not the needs of the patient in desperate need of the best care.

In this one instance in all of healthcare that I've seen, private equity is doing a much better job than other freestanding psychiatric hospitals. That's possible. I just don't think this paper demonstrates it because the data they had access to didn't have the granularity of information necessary to actually draw that conclusion. If you know anything about how a psychiatric hospital runs, which, for what it’s worth, I do.

I think the thing we can't say is that cherry picking patients is a great way of making sure your hospital is calmer, and at least private equity didn't make it worse, when they were allowed to do whatever they were doing to make sure the hospital could run in a way with less restraint and better follow up thereafter. It's not worse, but I'm not convinced it's better for the people who most needed it.

Thank you for coming to my TAD talk. That's like a TED talk, but it doesn't cost less, because I don't have anybody's brand.

2
